# Reading the Maven and Gradle Project Structure Generated by Spring Initializr

## Lesson Objectives

After reading this lesson, you will be able to open a Spring Boot project just downloaded from Spring Initializr and answer on your own: whether the project uses Maven or Gradle, which Java version it targets, where libraries are declared, where source code and runtime configuration live, which commands are used to test/run/package, and where the JAR file is generated.

This is the skill of **reading a newly initialized project structure**, not an advanced lesson on writing custom plugins, optimizing builds, or deploying to servers.

## 1. Understanding What Spring Initializr Generates

[Spring Initializr](https://start.spring.io/) takes options such as **Project** (Maven or Gradle), **Language**, **Spring Boot version**, **Group**, **Artifact**, **Name**, **Package name**, **Packaging**, **Java**, and **Dependencies**, and generates a project that can be opened in an IDE. Depending on your selections, the specific file names and contents will vary.

Consistent example throughout: choose **Java**, `Group = com.example`, `Artifact = demo`, `Package name = com.example.demo`, **Packaging = Jar**, and **Java = 21**. These are **illustrative values** for reading the structure; take the actual Spring Boot version, plugin versions, and package names from the project you downloaded rather than hardcoding from the example.

Two projects created with the same business options share the same core: Java code in `src/main/java`, resources in `src/main/resources`, and tests in `src/test/java`. The differences lie primarily in the **build tool, build configuration, wrapper, and build output directories**.

### Visualizing in Three Layers

1. **Project description and build process:** `pom.xml` for Maven; `build.gradle` or `build.gradle.kts` along with `settings.gradle[.kts]` for Gradle. These files determine plugins, libraries, Java level, and build tasks.
2. **Application:** `src/main/java` holds the main runnable class and business code; `src/main/resources` holds configuration/resources packaged with the application.
3. **Tests and outputs:** `src/test` holds tests; Maven typically generates `target/`, and Gradle generates `build/` when running a build. These two directories are **not original source code**.

## 2. Identifying Maven and Gradle from the Root Directory

A typical **Maven** project generated by Initializr:

```text
demo/
├── .mvn/
│   └── wrapper/
│       └── maven-wrapper.properties
├── mvnw
├── mvnw.cmd
├── pom.xml
├── .gitignore
├── HELP.md
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/com/example/demo/DemoApplication.java
    │   └── resources/application.properties
    └── test/
        └── java/com/example/demo/DemoApplicationTests.java
```

A typical **Gradle project using Groovy DSL**:

```text
demo/
├── gradle/
│   └── wrapper/
│       ├── gradle-wrapper.jar
│       └── gradle-wrapper.properties
├── gradlew
├── gradlew.bat
├── settings.gradle
├── build.gradle
├── .gitignore
├── HELP.md
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/com/example/demo/DemoApplication.java
    │   └── resources/application.properties
    └── test/
        └── java/com/example/demo/DemoApplicationTests.java
```

If you chose **Gradle – Kotlin DSL**, look for `build.gradle.kts` and `settings.gradle.kts` instead of the two `.gradle` files. If you chose Kotlin/Groovy instead of Java, source files may reside in `src/main/kotlin` or `src/main/groovy`. If you chose YAML, configuration may be `application.yml` instead of `application.properties`. Some supporting files such as `.gitattributes`, `HELP.md`, additional resources, or other wrapper files depend on the tool version and generation options; **do not treat the illustrative tree as an immutable list**.

**Quick reading tip:** see `pom.xml` and `mvnw` → Maven; see `build.gradle[.kts]`, `settings.gradle[.kts]`, and `gradlew` → Gradle. Do not decide based solely on the `src` directory name, because both use the same source convention.

## 3. Reading a Maven Project: Starting from `pom.xml`

`pom.xml` (Project Object Model) is the central file. Read it in order:

| Element | Meaning and Questions to Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `modelVersion` | POM model version, usually `4.0.0`. Not the application version. |
| `parent` | For Spring Boot templates, usually `spring-boot-starter-parent`: inherits pre-managed configuration and versions. |
| `groupId`, `artifactId`, `version` | Packaging identity of the project; e.g., `com.example:demo:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT`. |
| `properties` | Properties such as `java.version` (the selected Java version). |
| `dependencies` | Starters and direct libraries; look at `scope` to understand whether a library is for runtime or testing. |
| `build/plugins` | Plugins that act during the build; the Spring Boot Maven Plugin supports running and packaging Spring Boot apps. |
| `packaging` if present | Artifact type such as `jar` or `war`; when omitted, Maven defaults to `jar`. |

The following snippet is **only an excerpt illustrating which fields to look for**, not a complete `pom.xml` to replace the file generated by Initializr:

```xml
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>4.1.2</version>
    <relativePath/>
</parent>
<groupId>com.example</groupId>
<artifactId>demo</artifactId>
<version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>
<properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
</properties>
```

The version `4.1.2` here only illustrates where to **read the Spring Boot version**; the actual version depends on the time of generation and your Initializr choices. With Maven, versions of dependencies managed by Spring Boot usually do not need to be declared individually in each `<dependency>`. However, **not every dependency on the Internet is in the managed catalog**, and overriding a version can still change compatibility.

Example excerpt from the dependency/plugin declaration section:

```xml
<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>
```

This is also an **excerpt**, not the full POM. `spring-boot-starter` provides the core group of dependencies; starters for web, data, or security **only appear when selected or added**. `scope=test` indicates that the dependency is primarily for compiling/running tests. When reading an actual configuration, distinguish between **directly declared dependencies** and **transitive dependencies** pulled in by them.

### Maven Wrapper: `mvnw`, `mvnw.cmd`, and `.mvn/wrapper/`

`mvnw` (macOS/Linux) and `mvnw.cmd` (Windows) are the **Maven Wrapper**: they help the team use the Maven version configured by the project without necessarily installing `mvn` globally. `.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties` specifies the Maven distribution to download. Some wrapper versions/configurations include additional helper files; do not assume a `maven-wrapper.jar` must exist.

The wrapper **does not replace the JDK**: you still need a JDK matching the project's Java version and Spring Boot compatibility requirements. On first use, the wrapper may need network access to download tools/dependencies.

## 4. Reading a Gradle Project: `settings`, `build`, `wrapper`

Read three places in order:

1. `settings.gradle` or `settings.gradle.kts`: determines the root project name (e.g., `rootProject.name = 'demo'` in Groovy DSL) and submodules via `include(...)` if any. A simple Initializr project usually has a single project without multiple modules.
2. `build.gradle` or `build.gradle.kts`: plugins, `group/version` identifiers, Java toolchain, repositories, dependencies, and build/test/run tasks. `.gradle` files use **Groovy DSL**; `.gradle.kts` files use **Kotlin DSL**; syntax differs, but their roles are equivalent.
3. `gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` along with `gradlew`/`gradlew.bat`: the **Gradle** version downloaded/run by the wrapper. It is distinct from the **Spring Boot plugin version** declared in the build script.

Example **Groovy DSL excerpt** illustrating how to recognize configuration; an actual file may differ in plugins, repositories, dependencies, and tasks:

```groovy
plugins {
    id 'java'
    id 'org.springframework.boot' version '4.1.2'
    id 'io.spring.dependency-management' version '1.1.7'
}

group = 'com.example'
version = '0.0.1-SNAPSHOT'

java {
    toolchain {
        languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21)
    }
}

repositories {
    mavenCentral()
}

dependencies {
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter'
    testImplementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-test'
}

tasks.named('test') {
    useJUnitPlatform()
}
```

Version numbers in the excerpt **only illustrate placement**, not a requirement to update your project to those exact numbers. Do not overwrite the generated file, because Gradle/Spring Boot/plugin versions must be compatible. In the example, `implementation` provides dependencies for main code; `testImplementation` is for test code; `runtimeOnly` (if present) is only needed at runtime. Many projects also have `testRuntimeOnly` and tasks specific to the selected starters.

With Kotlin DSL, an equivalent example of a few lines of syntax is:

```kotlin
plugins {
    java
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.1.2"
}
group = "com.example"
version = "0.0.1-SNAPSHOT"
```

This is a **configuration snippet for recognizing syntax**, not a full `build.gradle.kts` that can run standalone. When opening Gradle in an IDE, the IDE must re-import (sync/import) the project to pick up the classpath, plugins, and dependencies.

### The Gradle Wrapper Is Not the Gradle Cache

`gradle/wrapper/gradle-wrapper.properties` usually has a `distributionUrl` pointing to the appropriate Gradle release; `gradle-wrapper.jar` and the wrapper scripts execute the wrapper. Do not confuse **`gradle/`** (project-managed files) with **`.gradle/`** (build-time cache/state, usually not committed). `gradlew`/`gradlew.bat` run the exact Gradle version chosen by the project; the machine still needs an appropriate JDK.

## 5. Reading the Common Parts: Source Code, Resources, and Tests

### `src/main/java` and the Main Application Class

With the `com.example.demo` example, `src/main/java/com/example/demo/` contains `DemoApplication.java`:

```java
package com.example.demo;

import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;

@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}
```

This is the main runnable class generated for a Java Spring Boot project, using Spring Boot classes available in the project's dependencies. `main` calls `SpringApplication.run` to start the application context. `@SpringBootApplication` combines startup configuration, auto-configuration, and component scanning. Components in **the main class's package and its subpackages** are usually scanned by default; placing the main class in too narrow a package can prevent Spring from finding components elsewhere.

**Distinction:** Java files in `src/main/java` are compiled into classes to run. The folder path `com/example/demo` reflects the `package com.example.demo;` declaration; the package name does not always have to match the Artifact.

### `src/main/resources` Is for Application Runtime Resources

`application.properties` or `application.yml` contains runtime configuration such as port, logging, integration settings, or application name. For example, you might add:

```properties
spring.application.name=demo
server.port=8081
```

The two lines above are only **configuration examples**, not present by default in a new project. `server.port` is meaningful when the application has an appropriate web environment; adding this line does not automatically create an HTTP endpoint. Configuration here is **different from** `pom.xml`/`build.gradle`: build files describe how to build the application, whereas `application.properties` affects application behavior at runtime. The resources folder may also hold `static/`, `templates/`, message files, schemas, etc., when the problem uses them; they are not required to be generated upfront.

### `src/test/java` Is for Test Code

A Java Spring Boot project usually includes `DemoApplicationTests.java`; a sample example:

```java
package com.example.demo;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;

@SpringBootTest
class DemoApplicationTests {

    @Test
    void contextLoads() {
    }
}
```

`@SpringBootTest` enables checking that the Spring application context starts in the test environment; `@Test` marks a JUnit test method. A test with an empty method body **does not mean no testing is performed**: context loading can still fail if configuration or dependencies are incompatible. A passing context test does not yet prove business logic or endpoints work correctly.

Directories like `src/test/resources`, `src/main/resources/static`, or `templates` only appear when corresponding files exist; their absence in a new project is normal.

## 6. Maven and Gradle Achieve the Same Goals via Different Commands

Stand at the **root directory containing the wrapper and build file**, open a terminal, and use the wrapper. The following table applies when the corresponding Spring Boot plugins/tasks are present in the project.

| Task | Maven (macOS/Linux) | Gradle (macOS/Linux) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Check tool version | `./mvnw -v` | `./gradlew --version` |
| Run tests | `./mvnw test` | `./gradlew test` |
| Clean output and build | `./mvnw clean package` | `./gradlew clean build` |
| Run application from source | `./mvnw spring-boot:run` | `./gradlew bootRun` |
| Output directory | `target/` | `build/` |
| Common JAR path | `target/*.jar` | `build/libs/*.jar` |

On **Windows PowerShell**, use `.\mvnw.cmd test`, `.\mvnw.cmd spring-boot:run`, or `.\gradlew.bat test`, `.\gradlew.bat bootRun`. On macOS/Linux, you may occasionally need `chmod +x mvnw` or `chmod +x gradlew` if the script lacks execute permission. `./` and `.\` syntax differ by shell.

The `package` (Maven) and `build` (Gradle) commands usually run tests alongside other build steps; if tests fail, the process may stop and fail to produce the expected JAR. For projects configured with **WAR** packaging, look for the corresponding `.war` file instead of always expecting a JAR.

### When Successful, Where Are the Outputs?

- **Maven:** `target/classes/` holds compiled classes and processed resources; `target/test-classes/` holds test classes; `target/surefire-reports/` holds typical unit test reports; `target/` holds packaged artifacts.
- **Gradle:** `build/classes/` and `build/resources/` hold compiled/resource outputs; `build/test-results/test/` and `build/reports/tests/test/` hold test results/reports; `build/libs/` holds the JAR/WAR when the corresponding packaging task runs.
- When **Spring Boot packaging** is present, `spring-boot-maven-plugin` or the `bootJar`/`bootWar` task can produce an executable archive. A Gradle build may simultaneously produce a regular JAR with a `-plain.jar` suffix: do not confuse it with the Boot archive containing all components needed to run. Read the plugin/task configuration and check the actual artifact names.

There is no fixed stdout string for `bootRun` or `spring-boot:run`: logs, port, versions, and beans depend on dependencies and configuration. Without a web starter, you should not assume accessing `http://localhost:8080/` will serve a page or endpoint. When running an executable Boot JAR, the command is typically `java -jar <path-to-jar>`; use the **exact file** that appears after the build.

## 7. A 10–15 Minute Process to Read a Newly Downloaded Project

**Step 1 – Extract and pick the right root directory.** Open the directory containing `pom.xml` or `build.gradle[.kts]`. If the IDE only opens `src/`, the build tool may not be recognized properly.

**Step 2 – Record project identity.** Find `groupId/artifactId/version` in the POM or `group/version` and `rootProject.name` in Gradle. Compare against your Group/Artifact/Name selections on Initializr. Note that the displayed project name does not necessarily equal the Java package name.

**Step 3 – Identify versions and Java.** For Maven, read the Spring Boot parent and `java.version`; for Gradle, read the Spring Boot plugin, Java toolchain, and Gradle wrapper. Then run `java -version` to compare against the configuration. **Three different things:** the Java version used to compile/run, the Spring Boot version, and the Maven/Gradle version.

**Step 4 – Inspect selected dependencies.** For example, if a web starter was chosen, locate the corresponding web dependency in the POM/build script. Starter names can change across Spring Boot release lines; trust the generated file and documentation matching that version, rather than assuming every project must have `spring-boot-starter-web`.

**Step 5 – Locate the startup entrypoint.** Open `...Application.java`, confirm `@SpringBootApplication`, `main`, and the package; inspect `src/main/resources/application.properties` or YAML. If the application does not yet contain controllers, services, or entities, that is normal: Initializr creates a **scaffold**, not business logic.

**Step 6 – Locate the default test.** Open `src/test/java` and explain why `@SpringBootTest` and `@Test` are there. If a test is not generated like in the illustrative tree, check your generation options or build configuration instead of assuming the project is broken.

**Step 7 – Use the wrapper to verify buildability.** Run the corresponding test command, then try packaging. Observe the results in `target/` or `build/`. If a command needs to download dependencies and fails due to network issues, distinguish download errors from Java source errors.

**Step 8 – Compare both variants.** Create another project with the same Group, Artifact, Java, Packaging, and Dependencies but choose the other build tool; tabulate which files are the **same** and which are **different**. Avoid comparing two projects with different dependencies or versions and attributing all differences to Maven/Gradle.

## 8. Common Misconceptions and How to Handle Them

| Misconception | Correct Understanding |
| --- | --- |
| `mvnw`/`gradlew` are application libraries | They are **build tool wrapper scripts**; not Java business code. |
| The machine lacks Maven/Gradle installed so it cannot build | The wrapper usually downloads the appropriate tool version automatically; JDK and network/cache are still needed. |
| A Gradle project must have `pom.xml` | Gradle reads `build.gradle[.kts]` and `settings.gradle[.kts]`; do not mix Maven commands into a Gradle-only project. |
| `src/main/resources/application.properties` controls Maven/Gradle | It serves Spring Boot **runtime configuration**; the build is described in the POM/build script. |
| `target/`/`build/` must exist right after extraction | These are **build-generated outputs**; their absence initially is normal. |
| `.gradle/` is the wrapper directory to commit | `gradle/wrapper/` holds the wrapper; `.gradle/` is usually generated state/cache. |
| Package name must always equal Artifact | Package is a Java namespace and can be set independently; check the `package` statement in code. |
| Having `@SpringBootApplication` immediately provides a REST API | The annotation boots Spring Boot; endpoints only exist when matching configuration/controllers are present. |
| `Unsupported class file major version` or toolchain errors are controller errors | Check the JDK used by the terminal/IDE/Gradle and the project's Java requirement first. |
| If two JAR files are built, either one runs the same way | Distinguish the executable Boot archive from a regular JAR; inspect task configuration and build outputs. |

## 9. Self-Verification Practice

Create or open **two Java Spring Boot projects with identical parameters** (one Maven, one Gradle) and answer using **specific file paths/names in your project**:

1. Which file confirms the project uses Maven or Gradle? Which file confirms the **wrapper tool version**?
2. Where can you find the Group/Artifact, Java version, and Spring Boot version?
3. Where are test dependencies declared? Why are they not necessarily on the application's runtime classpath?
4. Which line calls `SpringApplication.run`? Which file holds application configuration?
5. Run the corresponding test command through the wrapper. Which directory holds the test reports?
6. Run packaging, find the actual archive name, and explain whether it is an executable Spring Boot archive.

**Completion criteria:** you point to each file in an **actual project**, explain its role, and execute at least the corresponding test/build command in an environment with an appropriate JDK and network/cache. If the build fails, record the error and classify whether it is a wrapper/JDK/dependency or source code issue instead of only screenshotting the `BUILD FAILED` line.
